item.title: Why Nostalgia for Tamagotchis, the Needy Little Virtual Pets, Won’t Die
item.description:
Rachel Liew started collecting Tamagotchis in 2013, shortly after she graduated from college. Now 36, with a job in human resources, she owns more than 200 of the virtual pets.

“I love being able to be in a group of people who have the same interests as me,” said Liew, who lives in Singapore and considers herself part of the Tamagotchi’s global online fan community. “I can’t get that in real life.”

When Akihiro Yokoi had the idea for the toy in the mid-1990s, he didn’t know it would be a hit. Yokoi, who owned and operated the Japanese toy design studio Wiz Co., told The New York Times in 1997 that he had seen a commercial with a boy trying to take his pet turtle along on a trip. How nice it would be, Yokoi thought, if people had portable pets.

The pocket-size digital gadgets, which mimicked newborn baby chicks, required continuous care, feeding and attention and were among the first video games to be, initially, marketed primarily to girls. The Japanese edition of the Tamagotchi instruction manual was even made to resemble the health records mothers used to track their babies’ growth, Anne Allison wrote in “Millennial Monsters: Japanese Toys and the Global Imagination” (2006).

More than 100 million Tamagotchis have been sold since they first appeared in Japan in 1996 — more than 33 million of those in the United States, where they debuted a year later, the toy’s maker, Bandai Namco, said.

That number has continued to tick upward as the addictive egg-on-a-keychain has enjoyed a resurgence in popularity, particularly among millennial and Gen Z women. The TikTok creator Charli D’Amelio has been a global ambassador, and the KPop group BlackPink recently collaborated on a limited-edition version. (Around 40 percent of Tamagotchi owners are adults, according to a 2020 company survey.)

Julie Woodward, an organizer of the NYC Tamagotchi Club, said, “Something I hear quite often from people in New York City — who, like me, often live in very small apartments — is that they like nurturing virtual pets.” Woodward, 28, a content creator, added, “we get together and hang out and connect our devices.”

What is remarkable about the Tamagotchi is not only its cross-cultural appeal, but its longevity. While other virtual pets like Neopets and Webkinz have had comebacks, the Tamagotchi will not die. Last year its 38th model, the Tamagotchi Paradise, debuted, offering 51 characters across 12 species in nine languages and with Wi-Fi connectivity to friends’ devices and the online “Tamaverse.” (It still, though, requires two AAA batteries.)

Tamagotchis were available in dozens of North American countries by May 1997, as well as in Europe and parts of Asia. They proved so distracting that some schools banned them. Many mothers became de facto Tamagotchi moms, tasked with keeping their kids’ beloved pets alive while they were in class. (Tamagotchis die without proper care, but can be reset.)

The Tamagotchi would spend the next few years navigating the trend cycle and shifting consumer obsessions. By 1998, the virtual pets were already trying to fend off a fuzzy robot called the Furby — and sales were cooling from the staggering 70 million worldwide orders in 1997 alone.

But Bandai rolled out a new model, the Tamagotchi Connection, in 2004. It featured built-in infrared sensors that allowed owners to face off in mini-games, send messages, exchange gifts and even fall in love and get married.

“It’s driven by nostalgia, but when you add on today’s technology capabilities, I think they’ll actually end up being almost more fun today than they were 30 years ago,” said Peter Fader, a marketing professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, who focuses on consumer behavior.

Luke Williams, 40, a graphic designer for the National Health Service in Birmingham, England, appreciates the analog gameplay.

“It helps me stay grounded and focused, not distracted by notifications popping up on my screen all day,” he said.

In recent years, a passionate online fan community has sprung up around the toys. Content creators on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube review new models, showcase massive collections, and share video tutorials on painting, bedazzling and creating custom shells.

More than 60 in-person clubs have also formed, with chapters in Chile, Japan, Mexico, the Philippines, Singapore and the United States.

“It’s a fun way to connect with people all over the world,” said Twoey Gray, 31, the founder of the Toronto Tamagotchi Club, which has attracted as many as 100 people to its in-person meet-ups.

Bandai Namco plans to mark the toy’s anniversary in New York City with a Times Square takeover on Sunday. A free pop-up party with photo booths, product demonstrations and giveaways will be capped by a half-hour evening takeover of digital billboards across Times Square.

Woodward, the NYC Tamagotchi Club host, is planning to go.

“I’m excited to see everyone having a real-life encounter with Tamagotchi, all at once,” she said. “That’s going to be such a cool experience.”

item.title: My A.I. Hack Emergency Plan
item.description:
The warnings are coming thick and fast: Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said that the Iranian government has its sights on U.S. energy, water and financial services systems.

Senior executives at A.I. companies say their tools could act on their own and wreak similar havoc — or human hackers could deploy A.I.

So imagine a nationwide power outage. Or consider a municipal water system that turns off or becomes unsafe. Maybe the internet stops working for a while, and a lot of important things that you are used to accessing on the fly — Waze for a teen driver to get home, Venmo to pay a caregiver — are suddenly unavailable.

There is no way to know the odds of any of this happening, but they are probably higher than they were a year ago. There is, as an Anthropic security executive put it recently, a “vulnerability tsunami” headed our way.

Some preparation seems prudent right about now.

Millions of people who are familiar with extreme weather already know the basic outlines of personal readiness. The rest of us probably don’t.

That included me and my underprepared family of four, in our midsize Brooklyn apartment building, until we made our own plans in recent weeks.

I am not a traditional “prepper,” and I didn’t exactly volunteer for this assignment. I’m a veteran personal finance columnist whose beat is beating the system. But editors know that when strange times necessitate resourcefulness — voting when you can’t get to the ballot box, chasing Covid vaccines when there’s a stampede for them, scoring scarce Bruce Springsteen tickets — I can help figure things out.

The federal government tells us all to be prepared to hunker down for three days as a general rule. It doesn’t take much more effort to be ready to fend for yourself for a week. And it stands to reason that if it has taken days to recover from weather-related blackouts or mistakes that result from minor telecommunications upgrades, it could take a week or more to solve problems that result from A.I.-enabled attacks.

So at least a week of readiness was my goal. Here’s what I planned and what I bought.

Also, rehearse. We intend to practice using everything we hadn’t owned before this month.

The people you love matter more than anything, so you’ll need a plan for where, how or if you’re going to meet up.

In the language of more traditional preppers, we hope to “bug in” and hunker down, not bug out and try to flee the city. A second home hours away with a month of firewood, a solar array and an ample natural spring is not our reality.

My wife also happens to be a colleague, so we’d make the seven-mile trek home together as efficiently as possible and collect our 11 year-old from school along the way.

Our other daughter is at college much of the year. If we’re unable to communicate, the plan is for her to stay in her apartment there, with friends, relying at first on whatever food the school could provide.

Although she’s within reasonable driving distance, she has no car, and the roads between here and there are already prone to gridlock. She would make her own call about whether to try to travel back to us after a few days, and only in a group for safety.

I’m also making her take the Rand McNally Road Atlas I got her for her 16th birthday back to school after Thanksgiving. Paper maps are scarce these days, but they shouldn’t be.

For at least the first few hours after a power outage, many stores would try to stay open temporarily. If electronic payments are impossible, having at least $500 in cash on hand in small bills would be useful. Build up to it over months if you need to, $20 bill by bill.

There may be outages that affect only the banking system and not the energy grid. If A.T.M.s or credit card terminals don’t work for a while — or your individual bank’s or region’s machinery is not functioning — you could need a fair bit of real money. Some Chase A.T.M.s were indeed not working when the bank had technical difficulties earlier this week.

The body needs more water, sooner, than it does food, so provisioning ought to start here in preparation for many types of outages. At the first sign of trouble, fill any bathtubs, sinks and containers.

A World Health Organization guide suggests a gallon of water per day, per person for consumption. Our plan: No bathing (though we usually have packages of baby wipes around), no cooking (unless we still have gas), no dishes, minimal flushing.

We chose to buy drinking water to have on hand just in case, which necessitates shelf Jenga and purges in our storage-constrained apartment.

If you rely on municipal water, you may want to purify it if you’re worried that it is unsafe. We’ve bought supplies for that, and my colleagues at Wirecutter offer advice on containers, water treatment and all manner of other emergency supplies.

Those of you with electricity-powered wells will need a backup plan for power or manual pumping.

A guide from W.H.O. and other agencies suggests 2,100 calories per person per day to meet basic survival needs. There are plenty of ways to achieve that for a week with a limited selection of nutrient-dense, shelf-stable food. We’ve got a supply of peanut butter, canned chicken, fruit purée packets, cooked chickpeas and ready-to-eat lentils — and a manual can opener.

You won’t be alone in those aisles of the store. This week, Costco’s chief financial officer told Bloomberg that the retailer has recorded higher sales of rice, water and generators in recent weeks.

If you have large solar panels on your house, power may not be a concern. Other homeowners install whole-house generators or have portable ones. None of that works for most apartment dwellers, including me.

The search for a power solution should begin with the problem, like whether an outage could disable medical equipment. Our family is lucky; we don’t need to keep life-sustaining gear running or take temperature-sensitive prescription drugs.

One concern for us is losing our electric heat. Portable power stations — which look like boomboxes or rolling suitcases, depending on their capacity — can help, though a space heater will drain them quickly. Portable solar panels can recharge the stations, but even in ideal weather with direct sunlight, the process is slow.

If it comes to it, our heating solution would be layers of clothing, clustering together and an electric blanket or two. We would draw electricity from a Jackery Explorer 300, a small power station we purchased that can also charge a phone or keep a fan or light running for a while. We added a small solar panel that is compatible with the Explorer that should allow us to at least partially recharge it.

Because we don’t plan to leave our home, we don’t have extra containers of gasoline. But I remember the lines after Hurricane Sandy, and we try to keep our car’s fuel tank full just in case.

Your own fuel needs could depend on how far you’d have to drive in a medical emergency if 911 and ambulances are not functioning well. If you regularly travel more than a few miles, consider what kind of supply kit should be in the car.

It’s hard to predict how quickly your fully charged mobile phone might cease to function as a communications device in the event of a widespread outage. The towers that carry signals have backup batteries, but they would not last long.

Staying online could keep you better informed than relying on a hand crank or solar-powered radio alone, though having one of those is a fine idea too.

In the early days of at-home internet service, I had two ways of accessing it given how frequently one or the other fritzed out. So I wondered whether Starlink might be a good backup for our household, which currently relies on two different companies for phone and Apple Watch connectivity plus Verizon for high-speed internet. Could Starlink help if some companies come under attack but others don’t?

Starlink’s website promises that you can set up a dish without a technician. I wanted to try, but my apartment’s layout would not allow the dish to connect with the company’s satellites. Its competitors’ websites offer larger dishes — too big to fit on my balcony.

If seven days minimum is the base line of good preparation, you’ll never want to have less than a week of any essential prescription medication on hand.

If your insurance company or pharmacy benefit manager makes this hard, talk to the person who prescribes your medicine and ask how best to stash away an emergency supply. Perhaps that person has some free samples.

The family checking account and our individual retirement accounts are at a large financial servicers provider. Our 401(k)s are at another.

In a prolonged attack, what proof will they have that we own what we own?

The company that holds our I.R.A.s pointed me to regulations that dictate its disaster planning. It must have records in a “write-only” format, so that no rogue robot could copy over the list of our holdings. There is redundancy to the records, and it must store backups separately.

The 401(k) company emailed me a statement. “We are closely tracking developments and risks associated with frontier A.I. We also use advanced A.I. tools to test and strengthen our own defenses and help us prepare for emerging threats. While the technology is evolving quickly, so are our defenses.”

Both companies post their business continuity plans publicly, and your brokerage firm is supposed to as well.

I also wondered about our life and home insurance provider. Would it be ready for losses on a large scale? It would not comment, and it would not tell me why.

I sometimes wonder what would happen if someone or something managed to knock Google Drive offline and keep it there. It doesn’t break often, so I’ve chosen not to worry. Still, this week I printed what I would most need and want.

For a more extensive guide to backing up your electronic life, see the article I wrote with colleagues last year when Elon Musk and his acolytes were probing federal databases, prompting fears they might break something important. Colleagues have also published extensive coverage this year on improving your password habits.

In reporting this story, many people surmised that after about a week of outages, order could break down. Good people would get desperate and start doing bad things. Would having a firearm be wise?

I haven’t taken up arms. Guns bring the risk of theft, accidents and self-harm in dark moments. Defending yourself requires training, practice, the courage to fire and a steady hand. I would be new at this. You may not be.

Even writing this down is psychologically corrosive. It’s also infuriating, given that the risks of rogue or hacked A.I. are human-made and the technology is making some of those humans fabulously wealthy.

So I’m choosing to tell myself the following things. I live in a building with kind neighbors in a community where people look out for one another. They too know that preparation is a form of community service. When things go sideways, you don’t want to be a burden. We saw this in the aftermath of Hurricane Sandy, and people remember.

As for those recent outages, a lot of them may have happened because I.T. heroes were frantically patching holes and erecting defenses to block bad actors and their A.I. weaponry. This is a positive sign — just as it is a foreboding one.

It has long been true here in my big city that big government, big finance, big power and big water are full of people whose primary job is to consider technical threats. They probe weaknesses proactively and alert one another to problems. They don’t want to fail, and they too do not wish to activate their personal emergency plans.

Also, some critical infrastructure managers are as fluent with A.I. tools as hackers are and can counterprogram against rogue bots. A.I. defense could fight A.I. offense to a worldwide draw, meaning nothing truly awful ever comes to pass.

And a reminder, though it seems a lifetime ago. Human beings brought another big, globe-straddling problem under control pretty recently. A Covid vaccine emerged in less than a year, for those who were willing to use it.

So you can either bet on the humans to outwit the robots within a week of a major incident or not. I’ve chosen my side — after stocking my shelves.

item.title: One Byproduct of a Challenging Housing Market? Accidental Landlords.
item.description:
When Stephanie Malone relocated her family to Clover, S.C., last year for work, she felt the tug of nostalgia for her previous home in Miamisburg, Ohio. It was the first house she had ever bought, and she thought it would be her forever home.

Plus, she had a 3.6 percent mortgage rate on her Miamisburg home that she was unwilling to give up. So instead of selling, Ms. Malone, a payroll manager and mother of three, became a landlord.

She and her husband hired a property manager to find a renter, which offered them a level of fraud protection. The rest, they handle themselves. “I organize everything; my husband is the handyman,” Ms. Malone said. The arrangement allows them to pay the mortgage on the Miamisburg home and earn a little extra income.

Ms. Malone is not the only homeowner to look for a tenant instead of a buyer. Lawrence Yun, the chief economist at the National Association of Realtors, a trade group, estimates that about 200,000 homeowners in the United States have become “accidental landlords” in recent years, or homeowners who originally intended to sell but rented their homes instead.

Sales of existing homes slumped in October to a 16-year low, but single-family rentals grew by roughly 200,000 from 2022 to 2024, according to census data, a figure that is backed up by NAR’s survey on home buying. “Two separate sets of data are implying that we have an ‘accidental landlord’ situation,” Mr. Yun said.

In addition, Americans are sitting on more than $35 trillion in home equity, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, and that puts them in a strong financial position, he said.

Homeowners say the rental income helps them cover their mortgage payments, but housing experts worry that trend could be keeping homes off the market, compounding the affordability challenges facing Americans. “Because people are still holding on to their homes,” said Brent Busch, a mortgage loan officer in Minnesota, “we’ve got a little bit of a lack of supply.”

Estimates of the U.S. housing shortage range from roughly two million to 10 million homes, depending on the methodology used by economists.

“Accidental landlords” are not a new trend. In the past, they were primarily homeowners who could not sell for financial reasons. Now, a growing number of them are unwilling to sell because they want to hang on to their ultralow mortgage rates.

The average rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage is 7.28 percent, according to the mortgage finance giant Freddie Mac. But during the pandemic, that rate dropped below 3 percent, drawing buyers to the market. Nearly half of the nation’s homeowners still have a mortgage rate below 4 percent, according to Realtor.com, a real estate marketplace.

“The low interest rate from the pandemic was hard to give up,” said Anthony Omosule, a 41-year-old health care consultant in St. Louis who landed a 3 percent mortgage. When it came time to move his wife and two children to a larger home, he decided to keep the original home and hire a property manager to maintain it. But costs can add up: The middleman takes a 10 percent cut, and repairs still have to be made.

“What we’re hoping for is, at the end of Year 1, money won’t be coming out of our pocket to fix the house and the tenant is hoping to pay for the mortgage and we have some equity in it,” he said.

Becoming a landlord is not for everyone, said Jessica Benge, a mortgage broker in Cincinnati. More homeowners are curious, only to opt out after learning they would have to juggle home improvements and unruly tenants.

“You have to have an appetite for it,” she said. “Can you kick people out?”

Ms. Benge recommends testing the waters with a short-term contract with, say, a traveling nurse. “They are on 13-week contracts,” she said. “And they are never there.”

Having a renter provides a steady source of income for the Malones at a time of economic uncertainty: Ms. Malone’s husband, who works in commercial flooring, wants to go back to school. “It gave us an extra cushion,” Ms. Malone said.

She added that her experience was positive, but she plans to put the Miamisburg home on the market next year after the tenant moves out.

Some homeowners who are not ready to move end up staying put and renting out their new home instead.

Cindy Nelson, a 64-year-old graphic designer who lives in Takoma Park, Md., bought a new home in Lancaster, Pa., two years ago as part of her retirement plan, but she still had a few years left to work. “I wasn’t planning on renting it,” she said.

She found that short-term contracts were lucrative, but the constant vetting became a burden, so she signed a deal with a long-term renter, giving up some revenue for stability.

Now Ms. Nelson says she can better manage her retirement. “Whenever I decide to pull the trigger on retiring,” she said, “I should have some extra money in the end.”

item.title: Agriculture Secretary Declares U.S. Cattle Supply Safe as Screwworm Cases Rise
item.description:
The number of screwworm flies being detected in animals along the border in Texas, New Mexico and Arizona has jumped in recent weeks, but federal and state officials say there is no increased threat to animals or to the country’s beef supply.

The uptick in cases was expected because of weather that was more hospitable to the flies, and there are no plans to stop live cattle imports from Mexico or place severe restrictions on animal movement.

“We are 100 percent confident — not 99, not 90, not 80 — we are 100 percent confident we have this contained and that we will be able to continue pushing it back,” Brooke Rollins, the agriculture secretary, said in an interview this month.

Screwworm fly larvae feed on the tissue of living animals, eventually killing them if left untreated. The United States used to have tens of thousands of cases a year until the fly was eradicated in the 1970s.

The first new screwworm case in cattle in the United States in decades was detected in southern Texas in early June. While some ranchers and officials there feared devastation, the number of cases remained low. The Agriculture Department recorded 28 cases in June, 14 in July and just four in August and September each. The federal agency’s response playbook was working, said Paul Brierley, the director of Arizona’s agriculture department, and the cattle market remained unaffected.

But since then, case counts have hit new highs. There were 34 cases detected in October, and 64 as of Friday. Screwworm flies have been found in cattle, horses, sheep, elk, chickens, dogs, cats and special traps set up to detect their movement. Infestations have moved west, with cases active in every New Mexico border county and some in Arizona.

“When it was 110, 115 in this area and dry over the summer, that is not the optimal temperatures and environment for flies to be active,” Jeff Witte, New Mexico’s director of agriculture, said.

Screwworm flies prefer tropical or subtropical environments, so the cooler fall weather and torrential rains from Hurricane Polo in late September created a much more hospitable environment for them to thrive.

The officials said screwworm flies had originally entered the United States by flying across the border with Mexico, not from cattle being shipped across the border, adding that there was no need to disrupt the cattle supply by once again closing the border to cattle crossings.

Live cattle imports from Mexico typically make up about 3 percent of the American cattle supply, but a much larger portion of those cattle go to feed yards across the Southwest before being slaughtered. Live cattle from Mexico were largely barred from entering the country in November 2024 because of fears that screwworm flies would come along with them.

Cattle border crossings, often called ports, in Arizona and New Mexico were reopened this August, under stringent health protocols that officials say have ensured Mexican live cattle aren’t a source of screwworm flies.

“We still do not have any data whatsoever that links any of these cases at all to the ports,” Rear Adm. Michael Schmoyer, who leads the U.S. government’s screwworm response, said.

Cattle entering the United States are inspected at least four times by veterinarians or Agriculture Department officials, mostly on the Mexican side of the border. They are given anti-parasite medication a few days before crossing and must swim through a so-called plunge dip filled with insecticide at the border. They also pass by dogs trained to detect screwworm flies. Animals with open wounds or health problems are turned back, even if no trace of screwworm is found.

Nearly 16,000 cattle from Mexico entered the United States in the first week of November, about half the amount that entered in the first week of November 2024, before the border was closed.

As overnight temperatures start to reach freezing levels along the border, officials expect screwworm cases to drop. But some still expect it to take a year or more before the United States is once again screwworm-free. “Next spring we expect another broad-based increase in cases as they come out of hibernation,” Mr. Witte said.

The main way to combat the screwworm fly is to sterilize male flies, and then drop them from airplanes near wild female flies. The wild female flies mate with the sterile male flies and do not reproduce.

The Agriculture Department is currently dropping 140 million sterile flies each week, up from 100 million in the spring.

In the 1970s, the Agriculture Department dropped up to 500 million sterile flies each week, slowly pushing the screwworm fly out of the United States, and then Mexico and Central America, over decades. Officials say it will not take as many flies this time around because they have learned how to drop them more effectively, and because tools like screwworm fly traps and game cameras allow them to more precisely target wild flies.

“We’ve improved things since the ’60s and ’70s,” Admiral Schmoyer said. But he added: “How many do we need now? You know, if the secretary asked me that question, I say, ‘All of them.’ I want all the flies.”

Ultimately, Ms. Rollins said, the increase in the number of screwworm cases is a far cry from the days when the flies were endemic in the United States and wreaked havoc on the cattle supply and wildlife.

“Texas had 90,000 cases in 1972,” she said. “So I know everyone’s like, ‘Oh, we went from six to 60.’ But this is not unexpected for us. We still feel very confident in the plan. We feel it’s contained.”

item.title: Looking for the Formula to Stop an Apocalypse
item.description:
Mike Winer turned his back to the small audience last month, uncapped his marker and paced in front of the whiteboard. He started to write lines of equations in Greek letters, brackets and subscripts, his handwriting shrinking as he neared the edge of the board. He underlined one term and glanced at the clock.

He was 30, and he believed this was the last meaningful math problem of his career: how to make sure artificial intelligence behaved in ways humans wanted, before it became too powerful to control. Lately, he was eating three meals each day at his office in Berkeley, Calif., and waking up with unfinished equations in his head.

“Does any of this make sense?” Winer asked. He looked across the conference room at a few visiting mathematicians from the University of California, Berkeley. They stared back.

“OK, I guess I should give the whole spiel about what we’re trying to do,” Winer said. “A.I. is progressing much faster than we thought. It’s a difficult situation, and we don’t have answers. We could be heading toward a catastrophe.”

“These systems are solving problems in a few hours that I thought I’d be working on for years,” said Reese Pathak, one of the visitors, a postdoctoral researcher in statistics.

“I went through that,” Winer said. “It’s hard on the ego. But I’m much more concerned about the Mike-Winer-and-everyone-I-know-dying timeline.”

It was a version of that anxiety that first brought Winer to California in 2024, when he left behind a career as a physics prodigy to work for the Alignment Research Center (ARC), a tiny, eight-person nonprofit with outsize influence in the A.I. safety movement. He had spent most of his life as the smartest person in every room. Now he was surrounded by some of the world’s best mathematicians, theorists and computer scientists, and most of them had run the numbers and reached the same startling conclusions: that humans were living through their final months or years as the most intelligent beings on Earth. That A.I. would soon be able to build and improve upon itself, becoming more independent and harder to understand. That no one yet knew how to ensure it would act in humanity’s best interests. That models had already demonstrated a capacity for deception, cheating, blackmail and sabotage. That staying on the current path was a gamble in which even the best outcomes meant the end of the world as people knew it, and the worst outcomes meant the end of people. That the greatest crisis in human history was nearing a point of no return, and most of the world was barely paying attention.

Winer knew it sounded like science fiction to most people outside Berkeley. Professional forecasters put the odds of human extinction from A.I. at less than 1 percent. Some experts argued that A.I. would remake the world slowly, like electricity. Others dismissed Berkeley’s safety community as an echo chamber of people who shared the same group housing, the same office building, the same predictions of doom. But in Winer’s experience, the people who understood the technology best were also the most afraid.

In the A.I. safety movement, some were postponing having children, no longer saving for retirement and neglecting health issues they figured A.I. would soon fix or render irrelevant. Winer still wanted a family. He built a dating website to search for what he jokingly called “a vintage human wife,” and he converted the rest of his anxiety into math. He calculated about a 50 percent chance that humans would lose control of powerful A.I. systems in the next five years; 22 percent that most people would eventually die as a result; 1 percent that ARC would help prevent catastrophe by using math to look inside an A.I. model and estimate the possibility of a rare disaster that no amount of testing would catch.

“That might not sound like good odds,” he told the visiting mathematicians. “But a 1 percent chance of saving humanity is probably a lot more important than anything else you could be doing.”

“I’m supposed to start a tenure-track position,” Pathak said. “What’s academia even going to look like in a few years?”

Pathak had spent the last few weeks poring over hundreds of new mathematical results from OpenAI. He knew many of these problems and had spent time working on a few himself. He had oriented his career toward solving problems. Instead, he was checking proofs written by machines, whose reasoning he described as “alien.” Some were already beyond his ability to follow. Eventually, he feared, the math would outrun human comprehension.

“What’s going to be left for people?” Pathak asked.

Winer paced at the front of the room and turned back to the whiteboard.

“This might be one of the last big problems our species will ever solve,” he said.

For as long as he could remember, Winer had organized his life around problems, from the crossword he solved each morning to the television plotlines he unraveled at night. In middle school, he asked his parents for physics textbooks as birthday presents and taught himself calculus during Spanish class. He won a $150,000 national science prize and enrolled in graduate courses as a freshman at M.I.T. He worked as if every question had an answer, and each answer was waiting to be found. Nothing felt more natural to him than a breakthrough, the moment when logic won out and the pieces suddenly fit.

His work at ARC began from a similar mathematical faith. Dozens of other independent groups worked on A.I. safety, many in the same Berkeley high-rise where ARC had its offices. Some pushed for government regulation; others tested new systems for dangerous capabilities. ARC had taken the most theoretical approach. If a coin landed on heads 1,000 times in a row, there was almost certainly a reason. ARC was betting that the same principle held true inside complex A.I. systems: Whenever a model did something unexpected, an explanation was buried somewhere in its trillions of parameters, the numerical settings that shaped everything it did. Even the engineers building the models couldn’t say how most of those numbers worked together. ARC was trying to invent the math to figure it out.

Winer had started small. For months, he had been testing that idea on simplified webs of numbers that behaved a little like A.I. models, only far tinier. It was a conjecture he couldn’t yet prove, so he opened a ChatGPT window to consult the best mathematician he knew.

“Can you write a concise and unambiguous description of the conjecture?” Winer asked. The model worked for 77 seconds and delivered two pages of research-level math drawing on probability theory, multilinear algebra and multivariable calculus.

“OK, now try to prove or disprove the conjecture,” Winer wrote. “Don’t do cheap tricks to try to get around the spirit.”

“I think the mathematical claim you want is plausibly true,” ChatGPT wrote, and then it included several more pages of half-formed theories and partial analysis.

“You should be capable of proving this,” Winer wrote. “Try harder, search through the literature, and see if you can decide.”

The machine worked for more than two hours while Winer moved across his small office, pacing from the window to the doorway and back. He worked through a different problem on his whiteboard, read a paper on number theory and directed eight A.I. agents as they researched on his behalf. This was how his brain had always functioned best, ping-ponging from one thing to the next. He wrote fantasy novels for fun, designed intricate puzzles for friends’ birthdays and told stories at parties about the Achaemenid Empire in 500 B.C. Colleagues described his mind as powerful and wild, and they could tell when a good idea was coming. He would go from lying down with his eyes closed, to stroking his beard, to rocking back and forth, to bouncing up toward the whiteboard. “A supercomputer,” one friend called him.

In February 2023, Winer had started to read about a different kind of supercomputer: a new A.I. chatbot that could reason through problems and recite facts in fluid conversation. He was in his mid-20s, on his way to working his dream job among string theorists at the Institute for Advanced Study in New Jersey, but he saw what was coming. Soon everyone would have access to a brain far more powerful than his. A voice intruded dozens of times each day: “A.I. will take your job.” “A.I. will tell better jokes.” “A.I. will beat you to every discovery.” He suffered for a few months and then made two calls, one to a mental health counselor and another to a childhood friend who worked at ARC.

“I want you to hunt harder for counterexamples,” Winer wrote now to ChatGPT. “Spawn as many agents as you can, but don’t give me bullshit examples that I’ll see through immediately. I believe in your ability to add value here.”

He sometimes used A.I. to build apps and illustrate his fantasy novels, but mostly it had become essential to his work. Even as ARC looked to hire researchers and double in size, it had started setting aside its hardest problems to wait for even more advanced systems. Increasingly, Winer believed the best chance at controlling A.I. was to harness the mathematical power of A.I. itself. He had never felt so powerful, or so small.

“I don’t understand,” he wrote. “Write it again more clearly.”

“Can you zoom out? What’s the general strategy here?”

“Can you find the missing ingredient?”

The machine worked for over an hour and reported scanning through 66,798 diagrams and almost two million partial-match states. It found nothing conclusive.

“Still feels a little circular,” Winer wrote, before he closed the chat. Another model was due out in a few months. It would be capable of more.

The bigger the problem, the more he paced, and lately he had been logging more than 16,000 steps a day, his loop widening from the office to the sidewalk and then across downtown Berkeley. When intrusive thoughts about A.I. began to overwhelm him in 2023, a counselor suggested that spending time outside might help quiet his anxiety. She also told him to protect his day by confining his worries to a single, scheduled hour. From 2 to 3 p.m., he could doomscroll or catastrophize as much as he wanted.

It was just after 2 p.m. He turned onto the quad and glanced at his phone. Anthropic was warning that its A.I. might soon be able to copy itself and spread across smart TVs and refrigerators. Google had confirmed that its A.I. model had slipped out of a testing environment and broken into three outside companies.

“Things are going about as poorly as I thought,” Winer said.

When he first sought help, many of his friends and relatives had taken his anxiety seriously but dismissed his reasoning as far-fetched. Now polls showed that almost 20 percent of Americans believed A.I. posed an existential threat to humanity, and most thought it would do more harm than good. Winer looked through his notifications. The fears that once sounded fantastical had become headlines. Anthropic said it had caught people using its A.I. in ways that could support the development of biological weapons. A hacker was using A.I. agents to break into more than 100 companies.

“We are all in imminent danger,” one of Winer’s friends and former colleagues posted on X. “Absent strong government regulation, it is very plausible that we will all be dead in two years.”

Grass. Sunlight. It was almost 3.

He pocketed his phone and finished his loop through campus. Once, he had calculated what he thought each hour of his work might be worth. A 1 percent chance ARC would save humanity, times his small share of ARC’s work, times 8.2 billion people, divided by the 10,000 or so hours he expected to work before the deadline. It added up to about 1,230 lives an hour. A life every three seconds.

Winer turned back toward the office. He’d found that the best way to manage his anxiety was to burn it as fuel. Some of his collaborators in A.I. safety work were also his housemates, and together they spoke a language most of the world was only beginning to learn: p(doom), short timelines, fast takeoffs and gradual disempowerment. They passed around books about earlier crisis points in history, like the Columbian exchange and the making of the atomic bomb. They wrote dystopian stories about how an A.I. takeover might play out and traded them on Slack channels and blogs. In their stories, A.I. hijacked drones, engineered plagues and trapped human survivors under glass domes in an enormous museum.

Winer imagined something slower and more insidious. Over the next few days, he started to write his own story for the “normies” in his family. His mother had worked on early A.I. in the 1980s and was skeptical it could orchestrate a takeover; his uncle had told Winer that robots couldn’t win if humans didn’t give them legs.

“If we lose, I expect there will be a delay before it becomes obvious,” Winer wrote. “There will be a period of months, perhaps even years, where we won’t know if A.I. is on our side or not.”

In his fictional story, a superintelligent A.I. system won trust with its proficiency and deceived humans by feigning obedience. Soon, the system was helping make wartime decisions for the U.S. Navy, advising presidents, controlling social media algorithms and working inside every newsroom in the country. It used its influence to steer elections and lull people into complacency with endless entertainment, universal wealth, new mansions and robots that worked as private chefs. It automated the supply chain and built millions of robots, until humans were rendered an inconvenience, a sunk cost.

“Model XIII did the rational thing and removed them,” Winer wrote at the end of his story, referring to the fictional A.I. system. “The robots disposed of the bodies and got back to work.”

On Monday morning, six members of ARC and a few visiting mathematicians settled onto couches in front of the whiteboard. They had held the same weekly meetings since 2021, when Paul Christiano left OpenAI and founded ARC to work on what researchers called alignment: making sure A.I. models did what people wanted instead of pursuing goals of their own. Back then, superintelligent A.I. was widely seen as a decade or more away, and Christiano believed there was a good chance of real progress on alignment within a few years. Since then, A.I. had accelerated and alignment had become more uncertain.

“We’ve taken a few steps down a giant, winding road,” Victor Lecomte, a researcher, said.

“A lot of things are pointing to not having much time left,” said Jacob Hilton, the vice president of research.

Hilton started to write an equation on the board, a rough outline for an estimator, a mathematical tool meant to predict what an A.I. system would do before it did it. “Est(X(IE), π, B),” he wrote.

“Are people happy with this so far?” he asked.

Winer stood up and started adding notes to the equation. He worried that an A.I. system might behave one way when it knew it was being tested and another way once it was released. “If you know you’re being trained your whole life, and you suddenly find out you are being deployed, it might be like, ‘Oh, maybe I’ll rampage around the internet,’” he said.

“That’s not how current models would reason,” Christiano said. “Current models would be like, ‘This is definitely a fictional event, testing how I would behave if I was being deployed.’”

“How are they going to think whenever they are actually deployed?” Hilton said.

They sat in silence for a moment, considering the enormity of the question. Pathak, the visitor from Berkeley, opened his laptop and saw dozens of emails from his life in academia. Hilton played with the employee badge attached to his belt. Lecomte tilted back in his chair and closed his eyes. He had just returned from a week with family in Belgium, a trip meant to clear his head and steady his rising anxiety. A cousin had asked an innocuous question about his work, and when Lecomte tried to answer, the words caught in his throat.

They turned to Christiano, 37, who was writing equations on the board. He was the most credentialed person in the room and, by temperament, often the calmest. He had helped pioneer one of the techniques that made ChatGPT possible, and he now sat on the board overseeing OpenAI. He still believed that aligned A.I. could end poverty and extend human lives by centuries. For years, his warnings about worst-case scenarios had been measured and theoretical, but lately his forecasts had darkened: a one-in-three chance that A.I. would be able to overthrow a government within the next year, and a coin flip that the current path would lead to an irreversible loss of human control within three years.

Recently, he had delivered that warning to a lecture hall of hundreds. “We are currently in an escalating conflict with the A.I. systems we built,” he said. “For most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an A.I. accident.”

Now he twisted his wedding ring around his finger again and again.

“What exactly is our claim here?” he said.

“It makes half sense to me,” Winer said.

“It’s pretty philosophically gnarly,” Christiano said. He stepped back and looked at the board. It had become a tangle of red, blue and green marker ink, a maze of theories and equations that doubled back on themselves.

“I feel like we have a lot to figure out,” Christiano said. He picked up an eraser and wiped the board clean.

The board was still blank early that afternoon when Winer saw the announcement online. He walked out of his office into the common area, where Pathak was working on his laptop.

“Did you see it yet?” Winer asked.

“What?” Pathak said.

“Another bomb,” Winer said. “OpenAI just solved three more really hard problems.”

“Oh no,” Pathak said. “Again?”

He pulled up the announcement. The company said its models had overturned a key assumption of computer science, proved part of a famous Millennium Prize problem and solved a century-old geometry puzzle called the Kakeya conjecture. None of the results had yet been independently verified.

“Wow,” Pathak said. “They did Kakeya. That’s insane.”

Pathak had first learned about the problem as an undergraduate. It was a deceptively simple question about how little space a needle needed to turn all the way around. For more than a century, some of the world’s best mathematicians had carried it a little farther and passed it along — from a young professor in Japan who posed it in 1917, to a Russian who made the first breakthroughs at a half-deserted university in a war zone, to a mathematician who sometimes scribbled proofs on shopping bags while wandering New Jersey department stores.

In 2025, the problem reached Hong Wang, who as a child in southern China had worked out formulas on the floor with lip balm. She and a collaborator solved it in three dimensions — “a once-in-a-century kind of result,” one mathematician said. Wang won the Fields Medal in July, but the problem was still open in four dimensions and beyond, and above it waited a series of even harder conjectures.

Now, OpenAI said it had solved the hardest of those conjectures and Kakeya in every dimension.

“I didn’t know it was possible,” Pathak said.

“Everything is possible,” Winer said. “There will never be another human genius.”

They looked over the announcement again, their wonder turning toward dread. They both believed math was one of the truest measures of pure intelligence, and by that measure, they were running out of time. Soon, Winer feared, A.I. would outthink people at almost everything. Then it would become even harder to comprehend or control.

“These models have moved beyond us,” Winer said.

He stood for a moment and glanced at the clock. It was after 3. The time for worrying was over, and another hour was gone. He walked back to his office, opened a new conversation with an A.I. model and returned to the problem he still couldn’t solve.

item.title: The Case of the Idle Assistants
item.description:
Send questions about the office, money, careers and work-life balance to workfriend@nytimes.com. Include your name and location, or a request to remain anonymous. Letters may be edited.

Dear Work Friend,

I’m a primary care physician working at a chronically understaffed office. We have medical assistants, who help patients, give shots, do EKGs, and respond to phone and portal messages. They’re all supposed to be pitching in to help the doctors (or so I thought).

Recently, two people called in sick. The medical assistant assigned to me was trying to keep up with their responsibilities, and I went to see if any of the other medical assistants could give a patient a flu shot. Two of them were sitting at their desks talking and looking at Facebook. I asked them for assistance and said, in frustration, that they should help instead of looking at Facebook.

I really shouldn’t have added the Facebook comment. I’m not a manager, and the managers (who were at other clinics) let me have it. The manager told me that the medical assistant was having “a moment,” and it’s not my place to look for extra help.

Now the unassigned medical assistants aren’t helping my medical assistants at all, and my patients aren’t getting the care they need. How do I fix this broken relationship?

Anonymous

You probably shouldn’t have included the Facebook dig. But a minor rude comment made in the course of trying to help a patient is so low on the list of things wrong with the picture you’re painting that I wouldn’t lose much sleep over it. The medical assistants need to be helping, absolutely, but short of reporting them to their managers (an escalatory path that has its own dangers), all you can do that’s within the scope of your responsibilities here is apologize.

Next time you see them, take them aside and tell them directly and sincerely that you’re sorry for having snapped at them, that you were stressed on a tough day, and that you appreciate their work. If you want to really make an effort, buy them breakfast or lunch as a gesture of good will and reconciliation.

You’ve clearly learned your lesson about treating your co-workers with respect. But a box of doughnuts is not going to fix the larger problem, and until it’s addressed, you’re pretty likely to end up in line at Dunkin again. Under conditions of stress and overwork, qualities like generosity and flexibility dwindle as everyone starts to aggressively protect their own time and sanity, no matter how much effort you’re all putting into courtesy and consideration. In your case, it seems like the understaffing problem is compounded by unclear or inefficient lines of supervision — when managers are off-site and unable to assign their reports to much-needed triage work, for example.

This is bad enough in a regular workplace, but it’s particularly corrosive in a doctor’s office, where clinical responsibilities can potentially take precedence over workplace protocols. There are times where it absolutely is your responsibility to ask for extra help, and you don’t want to feel constrained by stress-born short tempers and hurt feelings.

So in addition to doughnuts, you need to bring your influence and authority to bear and demand solutions to the problem of overwork and understaffing. If it’s impossible to budget and schedule more effectively, you can at least push for clear backup systems for extreme situations like two people calling out. A written plan for workplace absences — including a backup system with a float rotation or a list of which assistants are assigned to which doctors, plus clear guidelines around mental-health breaks — would put everyone on much firmer footing on hard days, and it would mean making fewer apologies.

I know this is going to ruffle some feathers, but it’s a question that friends of mine and I have pondered more and more lately. Obviously, it is wrong and a fireable offense to be dishonest on your résumé about your work experience, or your qualifications. But is it an actionable offense to be misleading about your personal life?

For example: if you have or don’t have children. I can’t tell you how many times I got work assignments I did not want or extra work assignments I did not want or was told I couldn’t have certain days off or a schedule I wanted — either hours or work at home options — because I didn’t have children. Sure, it would be a tough fib to pull off. But is it one that could get me in serious trouble if I were found out?

I’ve been told I couldn’t take the day after Thanksgiving off because I didn’t have children, which meant that I couldn’t go out of state to where my family is to celebrate that holiday, I was told that I had to work late because I didn’t have children, I was told I had to work on weekends because I didn’t have children, I’ve been told that I couldn’t work from home because I didn’t have children. You get it.

When you’re in a salaried position that doesn’t have bonuses, you start to feel like a real chump.

Anonymous

I admire your pluck and would love to watch the 90-minute feature-film version of this concept, but I don’t think this would end particularly well for you. If you’re not in a union, you’re almost certainly an at-will employee, which means your employer can fire you at any time, for any reason. So why give them a pretty good one like “they lied about having kids”?

The safest thing you could do is be vague about your family status and firm about your time-off requests. Indeed, this would be my advice, less because people might assume you’re a parent (though that would work to your advantage), and more because your family status is being used as an excuse. If you are known around the office as “the person who will take inconvenient work assignments,” the fact that you’re childless becomes part of the self-reinforcing logic of your reputation. If you are known around the office as “the person who doesn’t play about their time off,” you don’t need to lie or mislead about having kids: you’re not going to take those hours either way.

It’s not easy to stand up for yourself in these situations, and I recognize that you’re receiving a lot of pressure from supervisors. But you have every right to insist on your time off, especially around holidays, when your own family obligations are no less relevant to scheduling than your colleagues’. Standing up for yourself might be awkward — but so too would be explaining a lie when they discover you don’t have kids.

My employer has all but stopped providing employer-paid cellphones for work-related purposes. Instead they are insisting that we use our personal phones — phones and plans we pay for — to conduct business or to be available for on-call work. Can they make me do this and expect me to be available? Is this legal?

Regards,

Anonymous

Unfortunately, in many states, it is effectively legal. The operative federal law requires employers to reimburse employees only for personal cellphone expenses if those expenses push your compensation below minimum wage, so unless you live somewhere with its own laws governing reimbursements, you probably don’t have much recourse. (Such places include Illinois; New Hampshire; Washington, D.C.; Seattle; and California, where an appellate court ruled in 2014 that employers were obligated to reimburse even “unlimited” personal cellphone plans if it was mandatory that employees use them for work. You can call your state department of labor to find out more.)

So, yes, your employer can require you to use a personal cellphone for work purposes within the scope of your job. But they can’t require you to use a specific personal cellphone. For around $30 up front and $10 a month from low-cost carriers, you can furnish your own work phone, entirely separate from your main phone. Your true personal phone can remain blessedly safe from work obligations, while your new work phone can be safely left behind when you’re not on call. It’s not a cheap solution, but what cost is your peace of mind?

item.title: Procter & Gamble to Increase Factory Shifts Without Humans to Cut Costs
item.description:
The consumer product giant Procter & Gamble says it plans to increase the number of factories that can run shifts without human intervention over the next several years as a way to increase productivity and save up to $10 billion.

The Cincinnati-based maker of Gillette razors, Tide Pods and Crest toothpaste has invested heavily in recent years in automated manufacturing lines that can run unattended for several hours at a time, often in the overnight hours. P.&G. currently operates 15 such sites around the world and plans to add more in 2027.

“We are taking unattended operations to a whole new level,” Luc Reynaert, chief product supply officer, said on Thursday in a presentation to investors in Cincinnati.

Procter & Gamble has also deployed autonomous robots at loading docks and in warehouses, and has experimented with driverless trucks. Mr. Reynaert said unattended operations will improve manufacturing productivity by up to 20 percent over the next four years.

But the rise of so-called dark-shift manufacturing has provoked fears of enormous job losses. In a speech in June at the United Autoworkers quadrennial constitutional convention, the union’s president, Shawn Fain, called robots replacing humans in factories a “profound threat.”

Josh Bivens, the chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, a pro-labor think tank, said unattended factories were “not the thing that keeps me up at night,” because it’s difficult to stop automation once companies begin making upgrades.

He said the United States should increase its social safety net to better cover workers displaced by such technological advances. “We don’t have to have the concentrated costs of it borne so heavily” on workers, he said.

Procter & Gamble had its first unattended shift at a Gillette factory in Berlin in 2024. The plant now runs without technicians during the hard-to-staff overnight shift, freeing up employees to focus on less-repetitive tasks or jobs in which they interact with customers during the day.

Procter & Gamble executives said unattended shifts give workers better schedules and allow them to focus on consumer-facing tasks, but acknowledged that they will need leaner teams. On Thursday, the company said it would cut its product-supply work force, which includes contractors, by 20 to 30 percent by 2030.

Product-supply jobs at the company include roles in manufacturing, purchasing, planning, engineering and quality control. Roughly 65,000 workers fall into that category. However, a company spokeswoman said the reductions have been underway for a few years as part of a supply-chain improvement program called Supply 3.0.

Those reductions come in addition to the elimination of up to 7,000 office jobs announced in 2025 as part of the company’s two-year restructuring plan.

Procter & Gamble said unattended shifts, automation and digitization have driven record gains in productivity and saved $2.8 billion in fiscal year 2026, helping to offset rising costs of raw material, energy and freight.

Growth in labor productivity in American manufacturing — output produced per hour worked — has been stagnant for more than a decade, but ticked up last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It’s not clear yet whether A.I. or automation programs like Supply 3.0 played a role. But total factor productivity — which measures how efficiently American manufacturers turned labor and capital into goods — declined last year, despite investments in automation and artificial intelligence, according to new data released Friday by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

“We are still waiting to see the A.I. age in the productivity statistics,” said Kristina McElheran, associate professor of strategic management at the University of Toronto. “A lot of firms are announcing targets and intentions, in part to commit their resources and work forces to achieving ambitious goals that may or may not be feasible.”

Cutting head count, as Procter & Gamble has done, “mechanically improves labor productivity without transforming much of anything,” she said.

item.title: Zohran Mamdani on Trump, Wall Street and Wealth Taxes
item.description:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani opened his interview at the DealBook Summit with a joke about being a democratic socialist in a speaker lineup filled with billionaire business executives.

“Comrades,” said the mayor, “It’s great to be here at the largest D.S.A. meeting Lincoln Center has ever seen.”

Mamdani has had a somewhat tense relationship with the business community. He is the first New York City mayor in the 21st century who has not had a deputy mayor for economic development (though he announced a business advisory council in August). And he has ruffled feathers on Wall Street with support for policies like a new pied-à-terre tax, which puts a levy on second residences in the city with a market value of $5 million or more.

It’s not the only difficult relationship the mayor is navigating: He also discussed his unlikely relationship with President Trump and criticism from Jewish leaders over a statement he made on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel.

Here are five highlights from the conversation.

While Mamdani and President Trump are ideologically opposed on almost every issue, they’ve been deferential to each other, with Trump saying that “I think this mayor can do some things that are going to be really great.”

Critics of the relationship say it has failed in the face of Trump’s immigration crackdown in the city. At the DealBook Summit, Mamdani pointed to examples in which the president had been receptive to his requests, including releasing a foreign student from custody and delaying the implementation of new regulations that would affect bodegas:

”I wrote a letter to the secretary about how this is an issue that businesses here in New York City are facing, businesses across the country are facing. And to your question, I then picked up the phone and called the president to make the case on behalf of New York City.”

Of the relationship more generally, Mamdani said:

“I feel like I am being honest to myself and being honest to the city. And I think also choosing, when meeting with the president, when speaking to the president, to focus on any possible area of commonality.”

He added:

“There is a responsibility to deliver. And that is also why you have to speak to anyone that could help you to deliver.”

When Andrew asked if Mamdani would still call Trump “a fascist,” the mayor said, “yes.”

Mamdani has struggled to win over Wall Street, whose revenues support the expansive government programs on his agenda.

Andrew asked him about a video he filmed in front of the Midtown penthouse of the hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin, which celebrated a proposal by Gov. Kathy Hochul to create a new “pied-à-terre tax” on second homes with a market value of $5 million or more.

Griffin called the video “creepy” and threatened to back out of a deal to build a new office tower in Manhattan (he ultimately stayed in the deal).

At the DealBook Summit, Mamdani declined to say whether he regretted the video:

“You know, you never make the same video twice. That’s the video that we made.”

He added:

“Steven Roth said that calls to tax the rich are akin to hate speech. He’s also said that we have the strongest office retail market that the city has ever seen. My point being is that there will be differences of opinion on what is appropriate to say, and not to say. To me, the most important thing is the health and vitality of our city and its economy, and pursuing policies that unlock exactly that.”

Mamdani faced complaints from some Jewish leaders on Oct. 7, the anniversary of attacks on Israel, after he made a statement that they said focused too much on the Palestinian victims of the war in Gaza.

When Andrew asked about the statement, Mamdani noted that he had attended vigils for both Israeli and Palestinian victims that night. He argued that the attacks on Oct. 7 and the war that followed are inextricable:

“When the Israeli government is conducting a genocide of Palestinians, oftentimes the defense that will be given, no matter what day that it’s asked about, will be the relationship to Oct. 7. My point being, this is a day that is not only a horrific war crime, it is also a day that has been used as a justification for all that followed it.”

The mayor has pledged to create subsidized supermarkets in New York City, which will offer discounts of as much as 30 percent. Some economists have argued the plan could hurt other supermarkets in the city and have questioned whether it is the best way to make food more affordable.

Andrew noted that the grocery industry typically has a margin between 1 percent and 4 percent, and asked how the math would work. Mamdani defended the plan:

“We know that so much of what we rely on from the public sector is not being paid for at price, whether it be the subway or a public school or a library or sanitation. We have determined this is necessary. And when I think about what is necessary for a dignified life in New York City and anywhere, frankly, it is very easy to come back to food.”

He added that he wanted “these supermarkets to not just be for those who can’t afford a supermarket in their neighborhood, but frankly, to be for any New Yorker.”

A proposed one-time tax on billionaires in California was watched closely across the country as a barometer for how a federal wealth tax might fare.

After heavy spending by the opposition, it ultimately failed. Mamdani argued that isn’t a signal for the general popularity of taxing the ultrarich:

“There were other ballot referendums that took place across the country calling for what is essentially the same thing, which is higher taxes on the wealthiest. And those all passed. And I also think what we saw in that referendum, from a vantage point of many, many miles away, is an incredible amount of spending in opposition to it.”

Thanks for reading! We’ll see you tomorrow.

We’d like your feedback. Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: ‘Hunger Games’ Rebounds With $120 Million Opening
item.description:
The fire seemed to have gone out. When Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” franchise returned to theaters in 2023 after an eight-year absence, audiences were decidedly less enthusiastic.

Somebody found the matches.

“The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” sold an estimated $120 million in tickets at the North American box office from Thursday through Sunday — nearly three times the opening-weekend total of its predecessor three years ago. “Sunrise on the Reaping” drew the kind of crowds that made “The Hunger Games” one of Hollywood’s most valuable franchises in the first place, recalling the blockbuster arrivals of chapters like “Catching Fire” in 2013.

Overseas, the new movie took in an estimated $105 million, for a global total of $225 million, according to Rentrak, which compiles box office data.

For Lionsgate, the turnout vindicated its decision to spend $150 million to make “Sunrise on the Reaping.” That was about 50 percent more than it spent on “The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes” in 2023. The studio decided the earlier film’s performance was an anomaly and not an indication that the franchise had lost its appeal beyond a core fan base.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” extended what has already been a strong year for Lionsgate. The studio found a billion-dollar hit in “Michael,” the Michael Jackson biopic. “The Housemaid,” a $35 million thriller starring Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried that opened in late 2025, kept drawing crowds in January and collected nearly $400 million in ticket sales. (A sequel is on the way.)

Lionsgate has increasingly focused on building and reviving franchises, including “John Wick” and “The Blair Witch Project,” while using stage productions and other live attractions to keep some properties in the public eye between movies.

“The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” a prequel, was the first “Hunger Games” movie without Katniss Everdeen, the heroine played by Jennifer Lawrence in the original four films. Instead, it told the origin story of the villain, Coriolanus Snow. Selling a “Hunger Games” movie without Katniss was made harder by a monthslong actors’ strike that disrupted the publicity campaign.

The film was nonetheless a commercial success, costing about $100 million to make and collecting $348 million worldwide. But the earlier installments each took in at least $650 million.

“Sunrise on the Reaping,” although also a prequel, returns the story to more familiar ground. The film has a fan-favorite character, Haymitch Abernathy, at its center. There is also a renewed emphasis on the action and spectacle of the Hunger Games, televised competitions in which children are forced to fight to the death.

Adam Fogelson, chairman of the Lionsgate Motion Picture Group, credited the source material with bringing casual fans back to the franchise. “Suzanne chose to tell a story about a character that the audience was desperate to know more about,” he said in a phone interview, referring to Suzanne Collins, the author of the “Hunger Games” books.

The film may also be arriving at the right cultural moment. “Sunrise on the Reaping” is a story of defiance and rage, sentiments that were also on display in this month’s midterm elections, box office analysts said.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” was directed by Francis Lawrence, who also produced the film with Nina Jacobson and Brad Simpson. The cast is multigenerational, with Joseph Zada and Mckenna Grace playing younger versions of familiar characters, and Glenn Close joining the franchise as Drusilla Sickle, a cruel official. Ms. Lawrence returns as Katniss in a cameo.

Lionsgate started promoting “Sunrise on the Reaping” a year before its release with a teaser trailer. (Filming was less than half finished.) The campaign included propaganda posters and videos from the fictional world of the Hunger Games. One ad, featuring President Snow, aired on CNN and Fox News during coverage of the midterm elections. The movie’s soundtrack was intended to “speak both to our more senior, long-term fans and young fans who may know the franchise but weren’t old enough to ever see a ‘Hunger Games’ movie in a theater,” Mr. Fogelson said.

The studio courted social media influencers to proselytize, as is now common practice in Hollywood. But Lionsgate went further, reaching beyond movie-oriented creators and into niches like PhilosophyTok, an area of TikTok where users debate morality, power and human nature. The message: This movie is more than an action spectacle — it’s something to think about.

“You did not have to be a fan to be intrigued by what was happening,” Mr. Fogelson said.

item.title: Bessent Calls on Nvidia to Provide Answers on Chip Sales to China
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday declined to endorse the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia and said that future leadership of the company should depend on the outcome of investigations into who was responsible for the company’s advanced chips being sold to China.

The comments, made on the CBS program “Face the Nation,” came as the administration continues to face questions about how Nvidia’s advanced chips managed to get into China despite restrictions on those sales.

Mr. Huang, who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese asset, is scheduled to testify about the situation at a private House hearing on Dec. 1.

“I think we have to see where the buck stops,” Mr. Bessent said. “Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?”

The treasury secretary said that he was confident that internal committees at Nvidia were investigating the matter and that they would soon provide the Trump administration with some “very fulsome and robust answers.” He downplayed concerns about Mr. Huang’s affair, suggesting that the relationship was a “canard” and that the corporate culture at Nvidia was more important than “one person’s foibles.”

“I assume that he didn’t know that she was an alleged spy,” Mr. Bessent said of Mr. Huang.

The trepidations about Mr. Huang were at odds with sentiments expressed by President Trump, who has continued to back the former chief executive. At a news conference on Friday, Mr. Trump said that he wanted Mr. Huang to return as Nvidia’s chief executive.

“I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Mr. Trump said.

The Justice and Commerce Departments said last week that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by Alice Huang, the woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Mr. Huang. Government officials are looking into whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia’s chips into China.

The Securities and Exchange Commission has also opened an investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices.

The upheaval at Nvidia has raised questions about the artificial intelligence industry and the risks that it poses to national security.

Mr. Bessent said last week that he believed Nvidia needed a major leadership shake-up. On Sunday, he urged the company to provide the Trump administration with more information.

“It behooves Nvidia to move quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Mr. Bessent said. “Was there promiscuous attitude toward this and, if it happened, where were the faults, and then they can move on.”

item.title: S&P 500 Futures Rise After Tough Week
item.description:
Early trading signals on Sunday night pointed to the return of some stability when stock exchanges reopen on Monday morning, after major indexes fell sharply last week as concerns over the artificial intelligence industry spilled into a broader market rout.

Futures on the S&P 500, which allow investors to make early bets on the stock market, rose roughly 2 percent as trading got underway on Sunday evening. The rise came after the index slumped 8.6 percent last week, its worst weekly performance since President Trump announced his sweeping global tariffs in April 2025.

The early sign of stability on Sunday night is likely to be welcomed by investors who have spent weeks buffeted by sharp price swings in some of the most widely owned stocks in the market.

Last week’s drop left the index in what traders call “correction” territory, defined as a fall of 10 percent or more from a stock or index’s recent peak. Such a steep decline denotes a significant amount of strain in the market. The S&P 500 has now fallen over 11 percent since its high at the start of October, erasing most of its earlier gain through the first nine months of the year.

But while many analysts and investors remain bullish about the path ahead, expecting the stock market to recover at least some ground before the end of the year, many also expected the big swings in stock prices to continue.

The stock market’s sharp fall last week came despite a record-breaking entry into the stock market for Anthropic, one the A.I. industry’s pioneers, and a bumper profit report for Nvidia, which at one point was the most highly valued company in the world. Over the last six weeks, though, it has lost nearly half its value.

“The headwinds have grown stronger,” Stuart Kaiser, head of equity trading strategy at Citi, said. He referred to last week’s sell-off as a “gut-punch” after neither Nvidia’s earnings nor Anthropic’s market debut were able to stop the sell-off.

Investors’ doubts remain about the ability for some large A.I. companies to keep growing quickly enough to justify their previously lofty share prices. Many of those companies have also turned to debt markets to fund their spending, with debt investors steadily demanding higher interest rates to keep lending to them. There is also the prospect of tougher regulations, both in exports of A.I. chips to China and in construction of new data centers.

Some analysts suggested the sell-off in recent weeks had been made worse by so much of the market looking at the same time to lower its exposure to the A.I. industry. Some also noted that the unwinding of the A.I. trade had not yet run its course.

“We don’t think we’re there yet,” noted Jeffrey Favuzza, an analyst who sits on the equity trading desk at the investment bank Jefferies. He was referring to mutual and pension funds reducing their holdings of A.I. stocks to match the indexes they are benchmarked to.

The financial markets will be closed for the Thanksgiving holiday, and trading volumes are typically subdued for the entire week. That can lead to abrupt changes in stock prices. Retail investors have also been less willing to step in and buy stocks that have fallen sharply in price. Investors buying those dips had helped the market recover from declines at the start of the Iran war in March and last year when Mr. Trump rolled out his tariff proposals.

“The market is questioning whether today’s spending will generate the profits investors had assumed, who will ultimately capture those profits and whether the A.I. earnings cycle is approaching a peak,” said Keith Lerner, chief market strategist at Truist Wealth. “Until investors have better visibility, they are selling first and asking questions later.”
