item.title: Built to Whisper, E.V.s Look to Mimic the Growl of Gas Engines
item.description:
When Lexus unveiled the next version of its LFA supercar last year at an event in Japan, the company said the car had been born from a simple decree by the Toyota chairman, Akio Toyoda: “No more boring cars.”

Mr. Toyoda had one closing demand, too, and it had nothing to do with horsepower, styling or price. He wanted the new LFA to “completely redefine the sound of an electric sports car,” said Simon Humphries, the company’s head of design. “When this car’s finally finished, it’ll answer Akio’s last request.”

The focus on sound was a bit of an eye-opener, if only because the new LFA — which might not hit showrooms until 2029 — will most likely be judged by track times first and track noise second. Still, the emphasis on the car’s sound was as much a nod to the original LFA’s V-10 roar as it was an acknowledgment of a future in which electric cars all have plenty of power thanks to the instant, and much quieter, torque of electric motors.

Electric vehicle makers looking to distinguish their models instead will be forced to do so with creature comforts, expanded autonomous driving capabilities, more driving range and quicker charging.

That list also includes the way the car sounds — both inside, where the cabin noises can be customized almost endlessly, and outside, where regulations play a bigger role but also where the car presents its personality to the world. Think bigger, more aggressive, engine-like sounds from performance E.V.s and more subtle tones from economy E.V.s and city-bound cars that aspire to be good neighbors.

Ferrari’s first all-electric car, called the Luce and revealed in May, uses an accelerometer to pick up vibrations from the rear axle’s rotating components, sound that is then equalized and amplified to create a distinctive growl that early reviewers say nonetheless won’t be confused with a V-12. For mass-market E.V.s, road and wind noises are often buyers’ biggest concerns, and automakers have focused more on producing quiet, with the Rivian R1S emitting a gentle electric-motor whir and the Chevy Equinox EV aiming to sound like not much more than a whisper.

“I think brands are looking for ways to make their brand stand out to make them more distinctive,” said Jasper de Kruiff, a sound designer and co-founder of Impulse Audio Lab, which has worked with automakers including Rolls-Royce, Hyundai and Tesla. “I think one of the most powerful ways you can do that is through experience, and then again, one of the most powerful tools you have for experiences is sound.”

For years, automakers have also been designing the sounds of their internal-combustion cars, too, especially on the inside, where luxury cars are designed to be calming, even spalike, in the way the cabin environments are tuned to reduce the stress of driving and riding. Mercedes-Benz, for instance, uses active noise cancellation in some of its cars, in addition to passive noise cancellation methods, including noise-insulating glass and a quieter air-conditioner, in cars like the new C-Class.

In electric cars, interior environments can be even more customized for owners and exterior noises adapted specifically to enhance the car’s presence, with automakers creating tailored sound experiences for each model in their all-electric lineups and spending hundreds of millions of dollars — or even, collectively, billions by some estimates — in hopes of setting themselves apart.

Automakers are tight-lipped about exact expenditures, and they have a policy of declining to comment on future products, instead preferring to talk about their newest releases, in part because before a car goes into production, key features of it, including the sound, could still change, and often do. But it’s clear that sound designs are getting ever more sophisticated and the stakes ever more higher with the proliferation of E.V.s.

“Sound is such a strong link to emotions and memories,” Mr. De Kruiff said. “I think it’s absolutely inevitable that we’re going to see brands dive deeper and deeper into that field and come up with some interesting solutions.”

Modern cars are also increasingly run by software, integrated with numerous autonomous driving and safety sensors, and outfitted with larger and larger screens everywhere, making the cars of just a generation ago look primitive by comparison. When it comes to modern acoustics, older cars are almost prehistoric.

In the new BMW iX3, for example, a template for the brand’s future E.V.s, the sound that salutes drivers when the car door is opened is composed of the voices of the car’s designers speaking about the most joyful moment of their life, which was then remixed and rehashed by BMW into a welcome song.

“So whenever you open the iX3 there is a subtle whispering of layers of the designers of the car that are speaking to you,” said Renzo Vitale, creative director of sound at BMW, making it part of the brand’s goal of “human centricity.”

Mr. Vitale, who is also a composer and pianist, said the iX3 was a compact luxury crossover meant to appeal to city dwellers and suburbanites. As such, it is meant to be “respectful of the environment” when it comes to exterior noise, the thing buyers are often most curious about. The iX3’s “engine noise” is distinctive but friendly.

“I like to imagine that the fact that my mother always told me that when you’re a guest at someone’s house, you should behave,” Mr. Vitale said. “I think cars are guests in cities worldwide, and they should behave.”

Regulations in the United States, as well as in China, Europe and Japan, also play a role, but many regulations came into force only in the past decade, and the way E.V.s sound is still very much up for grabs and thus worth fighting about.

Polestar, the E.V. maker affiliated with Volvo, has said pointedly that it doesn’t do artificial engine noises, full stop, preferring quiet. Others, like Porsche, have taken a less subtle approach.

“No other manufacturer has spent as much time working on the sound both inside and out as Porsche,” Tobias Hillers, who helped design the acoustics of the all-electric Taycan, has said about the German automaker’s efforts. The Taycan’s sound is an electric whoosh with hints of cars from Porsche’s past, like the 356.

Porsche had to confront a problem that every E.V. maker faces: Electric motors, on their own, don’t sound very good compared with the internal combustion engines of the past. “Anything that sounds like a dentist’s drill or streetcar has to go,” Mr. Hillers said.

Even so, internal combustion engines still exert a strong pull on car sound designers today since, for many of them, those engines were the soundtrack of their formative years with cars. Mr. De Kruiff said the 2003 Williams Formula 1 car, powered by a BMW V-10 engine, made probably his favorite car noises ever.

“It just gives me goose bumps every time,” he said.

His all-time favorite noise among passenger cars is a different V-10, that of the original Lexus LFA, an opinion that is not uncommon among car enthusiasts. Lexus probably shares that opinion, too, knowing that the LFA’s successor will have a lot to live up to, especially the roar.

item.title: In Vietnam, an Electric Vehicle Revolution Without Cars
item.description:
In Vietnam, life moves on two wheels. Tens of millions of motorbikes swarm the streets, carrying commuters to the office, children to school and delivery riders from one order to the next.

For generations, they have run on gasoline. Now, more and more are plugging in instead of filling up.

Soaring oil prices, a government drive to curb pollution and a new generation of hometown manufacturers are accelerating the shift. This year, one in three new two-wheelers sold in Vietnam is electric, turning one of the world’s largest motorcycle markets into a testing ground for the future of transportation.

The transformation is challenging an industry dominated by Japanese manufacturers like Honda and Yamaha, while creating an opening for Vietnamese companies like VinFast and Dat Bike.

And it has gained new momentum from a war thousands of miles away.

The United States’ war with Iran has disrupted oil supplies and sent the price of gasoline soaring, making electric motorcycles an increasingly attractive alternative. At the same time, authorities in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam’s two biggest cities, are pushing to phase out gas-powered vehicles. Enforcement remains a challenge, but the policies are nudging consumers toward electric alternatives and spurring investment in infrastructure needed to support them.

If government policy laid the groundwork, rising gasoline prices have given the transition a powerful jolt.

More than 973,000 e-motorbikes were sold in the first nine months of this year, a 91 percent increase over the same period last year, according to MotorCycles Data.

Around the world, surging prices at the pump have driven interest in electric vehicles. From Sydney to London to Rio de Janeiro, growing numbers of drivers are turning to electric cars, many from Chinese manufacturers.

In Vietnam, though, electrification is unfolding on two wheels. And local companies, not Chinese giants like BYD and Geely, are some of the biggest beneficiaries.

For Phung Quang Duyen, 54, the appeal was immediate. On a recent Sunday in Hanoi, a makeshift stand displaying Dat Bike’s latest model caught his eye. He circled the red motorbike, took some videos on his phone and climbed aboard for a test ride. Its acceleration was so powerful that Mr. Phung had lurched backward during the ride.

When he returned, he excitedly called his wife.

Their daughter was about to start her first job, and the couple had planned to buy her a Honda Vision, one of Vietnam’s most popular gas-powered motorcycles. But the Dat Bike cost about $1,160, roughly the same as the Honda.

And unlike the Honda, it would never need gasoline.

“Now I need to check and convince my wife,” Mr. Duyen said with a laugh, hurrying off with a packet of brochures.

For other riders, switching to electric is becoming an economic necessity.

Nguyen Van Sy, 26, rides a run-down brown Honda handed down by his parents. He relies on it to commute to his job as a chef at a catering company and to make deliveries for Grab on the side.

But keeping it fueled is eating into his earnings.

“The increase in petroleum has affected my work,” Mr. Sy said during a stop at a Hanoi gas station. Before the war in Iran, filling his tank cost about $3.90. Now it can cost as much as $5.41 — a steep increase for someone who depends on his motorcycle to earn a living.

“I am planning to buy an e-bike now,” he said. First, he needs to save enough to afford one.

For electric motorbike manufacturers, that financial pressure has translated into a rush of customers.

Dat Bike’s sales surged when gas prices rose 40 percent in March, said Nguyen Son, the company’s founder.

“We didn’t even have the inventory to sell,” he said. “It’s very clear that, eventually, we have to move to electric vehicles.”

But Vietnam’s electric motorcycle boom is about more than a temporary spike in gas prices.

Once dismissed as little more than souped-up versions of the electric bicycles and scooters favored by high school students, electric motorcycles can rival gasoline-powered models in power and performance. Many can be charged at home, while others have removable batteries that riders can swap for fully charged ones in minutes.

The expanding range of models is beginning to challenge the dominance of established manufacturers like Honda.

“In Vietnam, we’ve had more than 50 years of Honda bikes, so the change to VinFast or other electric vehicles is hard,” said Hoang Ha, deputy chief executive of VinFast E-Motorcycle Vietnam.

To ease that transition, manufacturers are pouring money into charging networks and offering sweeteners, seeking to overcome the fear of running out of power, a major barrier to electric vehicle adoption.

VinFast offers a battery-swapping program that includes 20 free swaps a month, enough to cover many riders’ daily commutes. The company says it has already rolled out 60,000 bright blue battery-swapping stations this year and aims to reach 150,000 by year’s end.

“At first you have to push people, and it takes time and costs a lot,” Mr. Ha said. He added that VinFast was willing to shoulder that expense to attract customers and encourage greener transportation.

Beyond corporate charging networks, a more informal charging economy is springing up.

In Ho Chi Minh City, some cafes let customers charge their motorcycles while they have a coffee. Enterprising families have begun selling access to their electricity, with some offering food, showers and even beds to waiting riders.

On a recent Wednesday evening, there were 20 lined up inside the home of Le Huy Hoi on the outskirts of the city, plugged into outlets along his living room wall.

He started his business two years ago, catering to students, nearby apartment residents and app-based drivers. Demand grew so quickly that he repeatedly moved to larger premises. His current home is the third location.

He, his wife and their two sons share two rooms. A third bedroom has been converted into a dormitory with 15 bunk beds. He also offers food and showers.

The business earns about $400 a month in profit. But even after expanding twice, Mr. Hoi said, he can’t keep up.

“As you can see, I am not able to provide the market demand,” he said, pointing to a line of bikes outside his front door. As he spoke, several more drivers walked into his living room, looking for a place to plug in.

For Dat Bike’s Mr. Son, the boom vindicates a vision that once seemed far-fetched.

Seven years ago, after he taught himself how to build electric motorbikes by watching YouTube videos, he pitched his homemade electric motorcycle on “Shark Tank Vietnam.” The judges were unimpressed.

“No one will buy it,” one said.

This year, as gasoline prices soared, Mr. Son posted photographs of customers crowding Dat Bike showrooms, taking numbered tickets and waiting their turn to buy one.
